problem: Prior outdoor navigation methods either rely on a fixed set of learned behaviors or terrains (GA-Nav, ViNT, NoMAD) or on slow remote VLM queries (CoNVOI). They cannot follow arbitrary language-specified behavioral rules (stay on sidewalk, stop for stop sign, yield) in real time in dynamic scenes.
motivation: Outdoor robots must follow scene-specific behavioral rules and react to dynamic cues such as stop gestures or pedestrians. Large VLMs are too slow (~6 s) for this, while learned policies need retraining for each new behavior. Splitting the instruction into a slow landmark-goal part and a fast behavior-cost part lets a lightweight VLM run on the edge at ~9.5 Hz.
key_idea: Decompose instructions with an LLM into navigation (landmark) and behavioral (action + object) parts, ground the behaviors as a real-time CLIPSeg-based behavioral cost map weighted by LLM-estimated action desirability, and plan with an unconstrained MPC that trades off goal, obstacle and behavior costs.
insight: Separating slow landmark grounding (GPT-4o, ~6 s) from fast behavior grounding (CLIPSeg) makes real-time rule following possible without retraining. Replacing the MPC planner with DWA lowers success (e.g. Scn.1-3: 80/70/60 vs 90/90/80) and BFA and gives worse Fréchet distance, so the cost-map-aware planner matters. Among VLMs, GPT-4o is best for landmark pixel localization (F-score 0.64 vs 0.44 for Gemini).
method: Instruction decomposition: GPT-4 splits the instruction into navigation actions, navigation landmarks, behavioral actions and behavioral targets (one-time).
Action desirability: a second LLM query maps each behavioral action to a desirability probability (stay on ≈1, stop ≈0), used as the action cost.

Behavioral cost map: CLIPSeg produces per-target segmentation maps S_i from RGB. The cost is c = p_i·S_i (p_i treated as the undesirability of the action), and the final map is the per-pixel max over targets.

Landmark estimation: GPT-4o is prompted with the RGB image and the landmark description and returns a pixel coordinate. This is transformed to an odom-frame goal and re-queried continuously (~3.6-6 s per query).

Behavior-aware unconstrained MPC: optimizes z=(r,θ,δ,v_max), the parameters of a smooth pose-following trajectory family, under J = w_goal·goal + w_obs·obs (LiDAR) + w_behav·behav. The behavior term projects the trajectory into the image and sums the cost map with exponential distance decay.
Extreme-action handling: if max(C_behav) ≥ c_th, v_max is scaled by (1 − max cost), which slows or stops the robot for e.g. stop signs beyond the planning horizon.
Gait switching: instructions such as 'use caution' or 'watch your step' trigger a lower-center-of-gravity cautious gait on the quadruped.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (LLM decomposition, frozen), GPT-4o (landmark VLM, frozen), CLIPSeg (frozen, real-time segmentation), plus an NLopt-based MPC planner
setting.action_space: continuous linear/angular velocity (v, ω) from MPC, plus a cautious gait switch

Scenario 3 (sidewalk, grass, pedestrians in colored shirts)

numbers_note: Real-world results only, per scenario (10+ trials each), with no standard benchmark. Only BehAV rows are listed; the DWA ablation variant is omitted.
results: On five real-world outdoor scenarios BehAV reaches 70-90% success versus at most 70% for GA-Nav and ≤60% for CoNVOI, with GA-Nav, ViNT and NoMAD at 0% in scenarios 1 and 3. It also gets the lowest Fréchet distance to human teleoperation in every scenario and ~76-90% behavior-following accuracy. The paper reports ~40% higher success and 22.49% closer to human paths. The system runs at ~9.5 Hz on an Intel NUC.
limitations: Sensitive to lighting conditions, which degrade scene understanding.
LLM/VLM hallucinations can cause wrong predictions; landmark queries to GPT-4o take seconds and need internet.
Only a small real-world evaluation (~10 trials per scenario, 5 scenarios) on a single robot, and goal heading error is sometimes higher than baselines.
